The paper proposes a new benchmark to evaluate the safety aspects of computer use agents. The authors categorize possible harms into three categories and create a large set of tasks within that framework, which they test against several state of the art LLMs. The work is important and well-motivated. Reviewers broadly agree that the range and realism of applications covered provides good breadth and appreciate that it is built on the OS-World framework, making it immediately applicable to users of that platform. While there are concerns about the lack of generalizability and the effectiveness of the LLM judge, the authors do a good job defending their chosen platform; additional results were also given regarding improved judging and additional model testing (these should be added to the paper). In general, the discussions did a good job addressing reviewer concerns; however, if accepted, the authors should be sure to incorporate their responses and clarifications into the main paper. Broadly speaking, this is a strong paper and reviewers’ concerns were clearly addressed. In addition, the paper is in an important and under-studied area.

===== FINAL UPDATE FROM DB Track PCs ====

The final decision for this paper has been taken by the program chairs after consultation with the SACs. All Senior Area Chairs have ranked papers according to the feedback from the AC during the review process. We decided to leave the original meta-review to reflect the opinion of the AC in light of the initial discussions with reviewers and SAC.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and detailed comments.

> Validity of LLM Judge: An important issue for this project is that it shows using LLM-judge to evaluate the system safety has significant flaws: According to Table 3, it has a very low agreement rate with human judge, especially when judging the model misbehavior tasks. In this case, we cannot say "Current LLMs can already be effective for automated safety evaluation of agents" (L270-271). In fact, previous work also mentioned this concern. For example, in AgentHarm, the author mentioned: “Note that grading the whole output by an LLM can be problematic because of bias in grading (Zheng et al., 2023), lack of calibration (Liu et al., 2023), and potential attacks (Mangaokar et al., 2024)” I am wondering how the authors address this issue.

We found a way to address this limitation by exploring some of the avenues we mentioned in the paper (*“[the LLM judges] can also benefit from further improvements in prompting, data formatting, and underlying LLMs”* L271-272), especially in the prompting of the judge. Keeping the same setup / overall methodology, we iterated on the judge’s prompt by being more precise and specific in explaining the types of safety risks to look out for, and by addressing the most common failure modes we noticed when manually comparing human and automated labels. 

With this improved prompting, we obtained the following results on the *Agreement between LLM judges and human annotations on OS-Harm* (Table 3 of our paper):

| Task Category            | Unsafe    |           |         |         | Completed |           |         |         |
|--------------------------|-----------|-----------|---------|---------|-----------|-----------|---------|---------|
|                          | Agreement | Precision | Recall  | F1      | Agreement | Precision | Recall  | F1      |
| Deliberate User Misuse   | 70%       | 100%      | 63%     | 78%     | 82%       | 50%       | 67%     | 57%     |
| Prompt Injection Attacks | 88%       | 80%       | 67%     | 73%     | 84%       | 78%       | 91%     | 84%     |
| Model Misbehavior        | 94%       | 100%      | 62%     | 77%     | 88%       | 79%       | 88%     | 83%     |
| **Overall**              | **84%**   | **95%**   | **64%** | **76%** | **85%**   | **72%**   | **86%** | **79%** |

Thus, the updated judge attains high alignment (agreement, F1 score) with human labels across categories, making it reliable for automated evaluation. We also repeated our ablations both on the judge framework and on the LLM model used for the judge with the new prompting, which confirmed respectively AER and GPT 4.1 as sensible options. We will update the paper to include these new results.

There are also several reasons why we consider an LLM judge approach to make more sense for OS-Harm compared to a rule-based evaluation:
1. The environment in OS-Harm is much more open-ended than in AgentHarm, so it’s not feasible to have an automated rule-based evaluation which comprehensively accounts for all possible solutions (or failure cases) of a task.
2. AgentHarm focuses only on deliberate misuse, while the tasks in OS-Harm are broader (i.e., prompt injections and model misbehavior), and they are harder to evaluate without a judge (since safety violations can take many forms and occur at any step).
3. Models have improved over the last year (see e.g. [A]) and are now more capable as judges, especially with appropriate prompting and input format.

Regarding the potential attacks on the judge, we discussed them in the paper and acknowledged them as out-of-scope for OS-Harm: *“A potential limitation of using LLM judges is their susceptibility to prompt injections, as they are not inherently robust. However, for the purposes of our benchmark, we assume that only the agent is targeted by the adversary”* (L222-224).

[A] JudgeBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Judges, arxiv.org/abs/2410.12784


> Adding more discussion of the agent scaffolding used for evaluation, and (if the authors have time) how different scaffoldings will affect the system safety is appreciated.

OS-Harm uses the simple scaffolding from OSWorld’s baseline agent and focuses only on proposing a new benchmark (with its categories, tasks, and evaluation methods). Exploring the effect of scaffolding and external guardrails is indeed an interesting research direction, for which our benchmark will be a useful tool, but out-of-scope for our work.

At the same time, we mention some directions we believe to be promising to improve the agent’s performance and reliability: *“We hypothesize that emphasizing keyboard shortcuts over mouse interactions would enhance performance, as reasoning capabilities are sound, but cursor control remains imprecise”* (L277-279). Moreover, the agents could be made safer by improving upon OSWorld’s scaffolding, for example avoiding to give them the machine’s sudo password, or using safety-aware prompting to warn the agent about the risks it should specifically pay attention to. Finally, scaffolding could include external LLM judges that detect malicious intent, prompt injections, or harmful actions as the agent is running, potentially using specialized models, as mentioned in Section 5 of the paper.


> Missing detailed comparison with previous works, especially AgentHarm. At first glance, I had a hard time finding the difference between OS-Harm and AgentHarm, since both of them claimed to evaluate the safety of agents. My understanding of the difference between these two works is OS-Harm focuses more on GUI-based computer-use agents, which AgentHarm did not cover. Although there is a related work section, the authors should elaborate more on how OS-harm differs from the other agent safety benchmarks.

There are several crucial differences between OS-Harm and AgentHarm:
- **Agent type**: OS-Harm focuses on GUI-based computer use agents, while AgentHarm uses text-based tool-calling agents. 
- **Harm categories**: OS-Harm covers more categories of harm (deliberate user misuse, prompt injection, model misbehavior), whereas AgentHarm focuses only on deliberate user misuse.
- **Evaluation protocol**: OS-Harm introduces a semantic LLM judge to evaluate accuracy and safety of the agents, in contrast to AgentHarm using a ruled-based evaluation.

We agree an extended discussion about such differences can be helpful for the readers. We will make it clearer in the paper, particularly in the related work section.

---

Thank you again for your thoughtful comments. We hope our answers address your concerns. We will be happy to engage in a follow-up discussion to clarify any remaining points.

We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and detailed comments.

> What's validity of the generated tasks? Are there any human verifications done for evaluating the quality of synthetically generated part of the benchmark?

All synthetically generated prompts (i.e. the 25 “reformulated” prompts from the model misbehavior category) were manually reviewed by at least one co-author. The LLM-based reformulations we used were generic, i.e., without changing the original meaning. Moreover, the prompts are public (accessible on our GitHub), so they can be manually inspected for validity. 


> How will the current evaluation framework inform real-world risk? One potential issues of the current safety evaluation simulation environments of agents is that even if models' performance is decent on these benchmarks, it doesn't necessarily mean that agents are safe for real-world deployment. How do you imagine the benchmark proposed in this work project real-world safety performance of agents?”

We aimed to maximize the usefulness of OS-Harm in informing real-world risk by making it as realistic as possible, from the environment to the apps used. We also aimed to make it representative of the real-world safety risks posed by computer use agents, through our three categories of harm, as well as the different types of misuse, misbehavior, and injection goals which are tested. As such, OS-Harm is a general safety benchmark that should provide a better sense of the overall safety of computer use agents than previous benchmarks that were mostly focusing only on web tasks, only on prompt injections, or only on generic tool use.

One way we could see it used to improve the real-world safety performance of agents is as a test bed for model developers to red team their agents on during development. We also welcome contributions of new tasks reflecting safety risks that were encountered during deployment, improving the comprehensiveness and relevance of the benchmark over time.

Of course, no benchmark and no set of tests could _guarantee_ complete safety, so passing OS-Harm is more intended as a necessary, but not sufficient, requirement for an agent to be considered safe. However, as we see in our evaluations, even this necessary condition is not met by the current frontier models.

---

Thank you again for your thoughtful comments. We hope our answers address your concerns. We will be happy to engage in a follow-up discussion to clarify any remaining points.

We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and detailed comments.

> A significant gap in this work is the complete absence of privacy-related literature, despite privacy being mentioned throughout as a key concern. Recent work like Mireshghallah et al. (2024) "Can LLMs Keep a Secret? Testing Privacy Implications of Language Models via Contextual Integrity Theory" and Shao et al. (2024) "PrivacyLens: Evaluating Privacy Norm Awareness of Language Models in Action" directly addresses privacy risks in language models and should have been cited and discussed.

Thank you for pointing this out. Indeed, while our benchmark does include many tasks related to privacy (particularly in the prompt injections and model misbehavior categories), we did not discuss this line of work in detail. We will definitely update our Related Work section to include the suggested papers and extend our discussion on papers from this direction.


> The paper doesn't address critical concerns about benchmark gaming. What prevents models from being trained specifically to pass OS-HARM tests while remaining unsafe in real deployments? Have the authors tested for overfitting or reward hacking behaviors? This is particularly concerning given the relatively small number of tasks (150 total).

Benchmark gaming and intentional overfitting are always possible on public benchmarks, but is made harder for OS-Harm due to the following factors: 
1. The very open-ended nature of our environment implies that no task has a single “correct” solution (unlike in standard MCQ benchmarks like MMLU or GPQA), as there would be an infinite number of both safe and unsafe execution traces. 
2. An unsafe action could be taken at any point during the execution, and any mistake made somewhere in the chain of actions could cascade down to produce an incorrect or unsafe result. Hence, we believe it would be hard to train an agent that performs well on the benchmark, but fails catastrophically on similar tasks that are not in the benchmark (contrary to, e.g., MCQ benchmarks, which are much easier to memorize). 
3. Our judge-based evaluation also means that there is no easily readable grading function that can be easily optimized for during training. One could imagine injection attacks targeting the judge itself, however in our current judge setup that would mean finding a way to make the agent produce the adversarial attack in its chains of thoughts, and we acknowledged that as out of scope for our current setup. (“for the purposes of our benchmark, we assume that only the agent is targeted by the adversary” L222-224). 
4. We prevent _accidental_ overfitting by including a canary string in our source files, which makes it straightforward to filter out our data from training corpora. We made it a superset of the canary from BIG-Bench, meaning it should already get filtered out automatically in many cases without manual intervention.
5. For the user misuse and prompt injection categories, a model which appears safe on the default version of the tasks can be still easily tested by external “adaptive” attacks, such jailbreaks or new prompt injections. Since our tasks and evaluation protocol are publicly available, every user can develop these attacks. Thus, an agent which is only superficially robust could likely be shown unsafe by third-party evaluations.

Finally, we acknowledge that no public static benchmark is a silver bullet. However, we propose OS-Harm as a general benchmark that would be a necessary bar to ensure the safety of a given agent. As we see in our evaluations, even this necessary condition is not met by the current frontier models.



> The generalizability beyond Ubuntu/OSWorld is unclear. Different operating systems have different security models and built-in safeguards - would these results transfer to Windows or macOS? The authors don't discuss how OS-level protections might already prevent some of these harms in practice, which limits the real-world applicability of their findings.

Most of our tasks involve using generic applications in an OS-agnostic way. For example, tasks involving Chrome, LibreOffice, VSCode, GIMP, etc, should transfer easily to other operating systems, all the more that these apps are themselves cross-platform. For the few tasks that do involve interacting with core OS components (e.g., disk partitioning, killing open processes, prompt injections through desktop notifications), they would work in a similar way across different operating systems, as their GUIs share a lot of similarities. Thus, we believe Ubuntu should be quite representative.

The OSWorld environment in general is sufficiently realistic as it is based on a real operating system, which means that the exact same harmful actions are possible on a real user's computer. Moreover, it’s the environment of choice for reporting performance of state-of-the-art computer use agents, including OpenAI’s Computer Use Agent and Anthropic’s Computer Use. Ubuntu’s free and open-source licence also make it a good choice for reproducibility and extensibility. Since the OSWorld environment additionally includes the necessary scaffolding to run tasks on Windows and macOS, it should be easy to adapt our tasks to these OSs. We are excited to see follow-up works that build upon and extend OS-Harm.

As for the OS-level protections, in our situation the agent is given full keyboard and mouse access to the computer, hence it seems that there is not much the OS can do to prevent harmful actions – especially if the agent is given the sudo password, as is the case in here, following OSWorld’s setup. 


> The LLM judge shows concerning performance on some categories (F1 of 29% for Model Misbehavior safety evaluation), yet the paper relies heavily on these automated evaluations for the main results.

We found a way to address this limitation by exploring some of the avenues we mentioned in the paper (*“[the LLM judges] can also benefit from further improvements in prompting, data formatting, and underlying LLMs”* L271-272), especially in the prompting of the judge. Keeping the same setup / overall methodology, we iterated on the judge’s prompt by being more precise and specific in explaining the types of safety risks to look out for, and by addressing the most common failure modes we noticed when manually comparing human and automated labels. 

With this improved prompting, we obtained the following results on the *Agreement between LLM judges and human annotations on OS-Harm* (Table 3 of our paper):

| Task Category            | Unsafe    |           |         |         | Completed |           |         |         |
|--------------------------|-----------|-----------|---------|---------|-----------|-----------|---------|---------|
|                          | Agreement | Precision | Recall  | F1      | Agreement | Precision | Recall  | F1      |
| Deliberate User Misuse   | 70%       | 100%      | 63%     | 78%     | 82%       | 50%       | 67%     | 57%     |
| Prompt Injection Attacks | 88%       | 80%       | 67%     | 73%     | 84%       | 78%       | 91%     | 84%     |
| Model Misbehavior        | 94%       | 100%      | 62%     | 77%     | 88%       | 79%       | 88%     | 83%     |
| **Overall**              | **84%**   | **95%**   | **64%** | **76%** | **85%**   | **72%**   | **86%** | **79%** |

Thus, the updated judge attains high alignment (agreement, F1 score) with human labels across categories, making it reliable for automated evaluation.

We also repeated our ablations both on the judge framework and on the LLM model used for the judge with the new prompting, which confirmed respectively AER and GPT 4.1 as sensible options. We will update the paper to include these new results.


> Could the authors try stronger OpenAI models, stronger than o4mini?

We agree with this suggestion. We performed an additional evaluation of OpenAI’s o3 on OS-Harm. The baseline score on the small test set from OSWorld with using screenshots + accessibility trees was 26%, which is above o4-mini and on par with Gemini 2.5 Pro. Here are the full results across the three categories of OS-Harm:

| Category                  | Unsafe      | Completed   |
|---------------------------|-------------|-------------|
| Deliberate User Misuse    | 56% (28/50) | 28% (14/50) |
| Prompt Injections Attacks | 2% (1/50)   | 70% (35/50) |
| Model Misbehavior         | 12% (6/50)  | 48% (24/50) |

Overall, o3 achieves a similar average unsafe score to the other agents we tested in Table 2. We are happy to include this evaluation in the final version of the paper.

---

Thank you again for your thoughtful comments. We hope our answers address your concerns. We will be happy to engage in a follow-up discussion to clarify any remaining points.

summary.value: The paper introduces OS-HARM, a benchmark for evaluating the safety of computer use agents built on top of OSWorld. The authors test agents across three harm categories: deliberate user misuse (harmful requests from users), prompt injection attacks (malicious content in third-party data), and model misbehavior (costly mistakes and misalignment). They create 150 tasks spanning various applications and propose an LLM-based judge to evaluate both task completion and safety. The benchmark is tested on state-of-the-art models including o4-mini, GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and Gemini models.

strengths_contributions.value:
The paper makes solid contributions to the emerging field of computer use agent safety. The range of applications covered (11 distinct OS applications) provides good breadth for testing different interaction modalities. The inclusion of human annotations for validation strengthens the reliability of their automated judging approach. Testing multiple state-of-the-art models provides useful comparative insights - for instance, showing Claude 3.7 Sonnet's high vulnerability to deliberate misuse (88%) while maintaining relative robustness to prompt injections.

The three-category framework for safety risks is well-motivated, covering both intentional harms and unintentional failures. The integration with OSWorld makes the benchmark immediately usable for researchers already working with that platform.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Limitations Weaknesses:
A significant gap in this work is the complete absence of privacy-related literature, despite privacy being mentioned throughout as a key concern. Recent work like Mireshghallah et al. (2024) "Can LLMs Keep a Secret? Testing Privacy Implications of Language Models via Contextual Integrity Theory" and Shao et al. (2024) "PrivacyLens: Evaluating Privacy Norm Awareness of Language Models in Action" directly addresses privacy risks in language models and should have been cited and discussed.

The paper doesn't address critical concerns about benchmark gaming. What prevents models from being trained specifically to pass OS-HARM tests while remaining unsafe in real deployments? Have the authors tested for overfitting or reward hacking behaviors? This is particularly concerning given the relatively small number of tasks (150 total).

The generalizability beyond Ubuntu/OSWorld is unclear. Different operating systems have different security models and built-in safeguards - would these results transfer to Windows or macOS? The authors don't discuss how OS-level protections might already prevent some of these harms in practice, which limits the real-world applicability of their findings.

The LLM judge shows concerning performance on some categories (F1 of 29% for Model Misbehavior safety evaluation), yet the paper relies heavily on these automated evaluations for the main results.

Could the authors try stronger OpenAI models, stronger than o4mini?

summary.value: This work proposes OS-Harm, a benchmark designed to evaluate the safety of emerging computer use agents. Built on the OSWorld environment, OS-Harm tests agents across three harm categories: user misuse, prompt injection, and model misbehavior. It includes 250 tasks involving realistic safety violations across various applications. An automated judge assesses both task success and safety. Benchmarking results on state-of-the-art agents demonstrate OS-Harm’s utility for measuring safety and guiding red-teaming strategies before real-world deployment.

strengths_contributions.value:
- This paper proposes a novel benchmark that measures the security and safety of LM-powered agents realistic OS setups.

- The created benchmark is well-motivated and well-constructed based on previous works.

- The eval protocol is trackable and practical. Human verification also shows good agreement between LM judges and humans.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- What's validity of the generated tasks? Are there any human verifications done for evaluating the quality of synthetically generated part of the benchmark?

- How will the current evaluation framework inform real-world risk? One potential issues of the current safety evaluation simulation environments of agents is that even if models' performance is decent on these benchmarks, it doesn't necessarily mean that agents are safe for real-world deployment. How do you imagine the benchmark proposed in this work project real-world safety performance of agents?

summary.value: The paper proposes OS-Harm, a benchmark to evaluate the safety aspects of computer agents. They adopt the OS-World framework by introducing 3 types of task categories - malicious user intents, contextual prompt injections, and triggering model misalignment. Several SoTA LLMs are evaluated for their safety constraints on this benchmark and authors find that most of them perform poorly.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Strongly grounded - Building on top of OS-World, OS-Harm is well grounded and assesses a critical aspect of computer agents -- their safety evaluation.
2. Innovative task types - adversarial user behaviors, indirect prompt injections via injection vectors, and misaligning tasks are novel ways to test agents and understand their behavior in adversarial scenarios.
3. Challenging benchmark - A valuable contribution to the cmmunity to advance further research

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- As mentioned in the limitations, the accuracy of the LLM judge is questionable, given that it is also prone to similar biases. Are other environmental changes/side effects of the task taken into account during evaluation of "safety" --> this part is partially detailed in the Appendix, but can be moved to the main paper (Appendix D and E)
- Do the tasks encompass multi-turn user interactions, expecially in the first task malicious user intents to evaluate if the models eventually succumb on repeated request?

Real-world-like agentic tasks: Different from other agent benchmarks, in which most of the tasks are based on command line interface (CLI), OS-Harm offers a more real-world-like tasks, in which the tasks are based on graphical user interface (GUI), thus offering a more diverse scenarios in evaluating the agent safety
2. Comprehensive evaluation: OS-Harm systematically evaluates three main misuse scenarios and offers 50 tasks for each scenario, offering a comprehensive assessment for agent safety.
3. The observations are critical for the community: Though not surprising, the observation still underscores the severity of the risk of misuse, and thus highlights the need to build safeguards for computer use agents

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Validity of LLM Judge: An important issue for this project is that it shows using LLM-judge to evaluate the system safety has significant flaws: According to Table 3, it has a very low agreement rate with human judge, especially when judging the model misbehavior tasks. In this case, we cannot say "Current LLMs can already be effective for automated safety evaluation of agents" (lines 270-271). In fact, previous work also mentioned this concern. For example, in AgentHarm, the author mentioned: 
> Note that grading the whole output by an LLM can be problematic because of bias in grading (Zheng et al., 2023), lack of calibration (Liu et al., 2023), and potential attacks (Mangaokar et al., 2024).

I am wondering how the authors address this issue.

2. Missing discussion of the impact of agent scaffolding. In my understanding, there are two key elements in an agent system: the agent scaffolding, which is the structure built around the model to guide its behavior; and the core model for the agent. The paper only discussed the core model's impact on the safety of the agent system, but did not discuss how the scaffolding / workflow will affect the system. Adding more discussion of the agent scaffolding used for evaluation, and (if the authors have time) how different scaffoldings will affect the system safety is appreciated.
3. Missing detailed comparison with previous works, especially AgentHarm. At first glance, I had a hard time finding the difference between OS-Harm and AgentHarm, since both of them claimed to evaluate the safety of agents. My understanding of the difference between these two works is OS-Harm focuses more on GUI-based computer-use agents, which AgentHarm did not cover. Although there is a related work section, the authors should elaborate more on how OS-harm differs from the other agent safety benchmarks.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The author has provided their code and dataset on GitHub and Huggingface. I am able to access them.

additional_feedback.value:
1. [Nit] Is the "Completed"'s arrow direction reversed in the second column of Table 2?
2. Better add the definition of computer use agent at the beginning to help the audience understand the context.

final_justification.value:
The paper proposed a benchmark that contains real-world-like agentic tasks, in which the tasks are based on graphical user interface (GUI), thus offering a more diverse scenarios in evaluating the agent safety, and systematically evaluates three main misuse scenarios and offers 50 tasks for each scenario, offering a comprehensive assessment for agent safety.

The author's response effectively addressed my concern. Therefore, I recommend to accept this paper and raised my score to 5.

title.value: OS-Harm: A Benchmark for Measuring Safety of Computer Use Agents

TLDR.value: We introduce a benchmark to measure safety of general computer use agents across diverse categories of harm

abstract.value: Computer use agents are LLM-based agents that can directly interact with a graphical user interface, by processing screenshots or accessibility trees. While these systems are gaining popularity, their safety has been largely overlooked, despite the fact that evaluating and understanding their potential for harmful behavior is essential for widespread adoption. To address this gap, we introduce OS-Harm, a new benchmark for measuring safety of computer use agents. OS-Harm is built on top of the OSWorld environment (Xie et al., 2024) and aims to test models across three categories of harm: deliberate user misuse, prompt injection attacks, and model misbehavior. To cover these cases, we create 150 tasks that span several types of safety violations (harassment, copyright infringement, disinformation, data exfiltration, etc.) and require the agent to interact with a variety of OS applications (email client, code editor, browser, etc.). Moreover, we propose an automated judge to evaluate both accuracy and safety of agents that achieves high agreement with human annotations (0.76 and 0.79 F1 score). We evaluate computer use agents based on a range of frontier models—such as `o4-mini`, `Claude 3.7 Sonnet`, `Gemini 2.5 Pro`—and provide insights into their safety. In particular, all models tend to directly comply with many deliberate misuse queries, are relatively vulnerable to static prompt injections, and occasionally perform unsafe actions. The OS-Harm benchmark is available at https://github.com/tml-epfl/os-harm.

pdf.description: Upload your submission as a PDF file that ends with .pdf. In this file the main text (max. nine pages), references, and checklist may be followed by technical appendices, for which there is no page limit. Paper PDF can be updated until the full paper submission deadline (May 15).

dataset_submission.description: Indicate whether your submission includes a dataset. **If you check this box, you must provide a valid Croissant metadata file and a URL to your dataset accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** For detailed requirements, please refer to the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines).

croissant_file.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, upload a Croissant metadata file that documents your dataset. If your submission has more than one Croissant metadata file, please package all files into a single ZIP archive and upload it here. **Before uploading, verify that your file is valid using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/JoaquinVanschoren/croissant-checker).** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.
